h1: Beer with mutton curry and slow cooked Indian meat dishes
title: Beer with Mutton Curry and Slow Cooking | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer pairings for mutton curry, laal maas, nihari, kosha mangsho and other slow cooked Indian meat dishes, with styles that suit each gravy.
teaser: Hours on the stove give mutton curry its depth. Here are the beers with enough body to keep up.
standfirst: Slow cooked mutton is the Sunday dish in homes across India. Long cooking builds deep, browned, spiced flavours that make light beers taste like water. Here is how we would choose a beer with the weight to match.
sections: Slow cooking builds flavours beer can meet

In India, mutton almost always means goat. It is lean but full of connective tissue, so it is cooked slowly until the collagen breaks down into gelatine. That gives the gravy its body. Onions are browned for a long time. Whole spices are fried in oil or ghee. Browning creates the same family of toasty, roasted flavours that kilning creates in malt.

That is the key to pairing. A beer with toasted, caramel or roasted malt has a natural link to a browned onion gravy. Light, pale lagers do not. They are refreshing but they vanish next to a curry that has been on the stove for two hours.
Home style mutton curry wants a brown ale

The everyday mutton curry, with onion, tomato, ginger, garlic and garam masala, varies from house to house but is always rich and savoury. Our first choice is an English brown ale or a dunkel at 4.5 to 5.5% ABV. Their nutty, bready malt matches the browned onion. Bitterness of about 20 to 30 IBU is enough to stop the fat from coating your mouth.

An amber lager or a Märzen is the lighter option if you prefer lager. If you like dark beer, a dry stout works surprisingly well, its roast echoing the deeply cooked masala.
Laal maas needs a softer touch

Rajasthan's laal maas is mutton cooked with a large amount of dried red chillies, traditionally Mathania chillies, along with yoghurt, garlic and ghee. It is fiery, smoky and rich. Some cooks finish it with dhungar, a smoking technique where hot charcoal is placed in a bowl of ghee inside the covered pot.

With this much chilli, roast and hop bitterness can make the burn worse. We would choose a Märzen or a Vienna lager, whose malt sweetness calms the heat. A hefeweizen is the gentler option still, at only 8 to 15 IBU. If the dish has the dhungar smoke, a mild smoked beer is a bold match for the brave.

Nihari is a slow cooked stew of mutton or beef shank, traditionally cooked overnight and eaten at breakfast in Old Delhi and Lucknow. Its gravy is thick with bone marrow and wheat flour, perfumed with a special spice blend. Korma and raan (a whole slow roasted leg of lamb) belong to the same rich family.

These are heavy, silky and aromatic. A Belgian dubbel, with dried fruit and caramel notes, suits the warm spice. At 6 to 7.5% ABV it should be a small glass. A Scotch ale or a strong brown ale works in the same way. If you want something lighter, a Märzen carries enough malt without the strength.
Kosha mangsho and the eastern curries

Bengal's kosha mangsho is mutton cooked slowly with mustard oil, onion and spices until the gravy reduces and clings to the meat. Kosha means sautéed or stirred. The mustard oil gives a pungent edge that sets it apart from northern curries.

Mustard pungency and hop bitterness can clash. A brown ale or a dunkel with only moderate bitterness is the safer match. A porter at around 5% ABV is also good, especially with luchi on the side. Odisha's mutton curry with potatoes and Goa's xacuti, with roasted coconut and poppy seed, follow similar logic: toasted malt with toasted spice.

Mutton biryani and yakhni pulao use the same meat but behave differently. The rice soaks up the flavours, while the spices are more aromatic and less heavy. Fried onion, saffron, mint and rose water lift the dish.

Here an amber lager or a Märzen is right. A witbier is a lovely match with yakhni pulao, whose fennel and whole spices sit beside the beer's coriander and orange. Our guide to Indian food and beer pairing covers biryani styles from different regions.

Dry dishes such as mutton sukka, bhuna gosht and keema behave more like grilled meat than curry. With less gravy, the spice sits right on the meat and the browning is more intense. A Vienna lager or a brown ale both work, though a dry stout is worth a try with bhuna gosht. Keema pav, with its buttered bread, is happy with almost any amber beer.
Serve darker beers a little warmer

Brown ales, dunkels, porters and dubbels taste best at 8 to 13 °C, not straight from a fridge at 3 °C. Cold hides the malt flavour you chose them for. Take them out of the fridge 15 to 20 minutes before dinner in an Indian kitchen. In summer it will take less.

Try one test at home. Pour a pale lager and a brown ale, both at their right temperature. Taste each with the same spoonful of mutton curry. The lager will feel thin. The brown ale will taste as if it belongs in the meal. Learning to spot that link between browned food and malt is the start of pairing well.

Your first step: this Sunday, swap the usual lager for a brown ale or a dunkel with your mutton curry. Let it warm a little before you pour.
faqs: What beer goes best with mutton curry?
A brown ale or dunkel at 4.5 to 5.5% ABV. Their nutty, bready malt matches the browned onion gravy while moderate bitterness cuts the fat.
What beer suits fiery laal maas?
A Märzen, Vienna lager or hefeweizen. Malt sweetness and low bitterness calm the heat of the dried red chillies.
Should dark beer be served ice cold?
No. Brown ales, porters and dubbels show their malt best at 8 to 13 °C. Very cold temperatures hide the flavours you want with rich food.
